title: Help Willow, 6, Reach Her Brain Tumour Trial in Germany
description: Willow, 6, has been diagnosed with diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DIPG) — an aggressive childhood brainstem tumour. She urgently needs a specialist immunotherapy and targeted-therapy trial programme in Germany — treatment that is not funded by the NHS.

images.alt: Willow on a quiet morning at home

story.intro: Willow is a 6-year-old Year 2 pupil from Leeds who was diagnosed with diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DIPG), H3 K27M-mutant — an aggressive tumour of the brainstem that affects around 40 children a year in the UK. Standard radiotherapy can buy months, but it cannot cure her. The only active option left — a specialist trial immunotherapy programme in Germany — is not funded by the NHS.

sections.title: The Diagnosis
sections.content:
It started in August 2026 with a squint in her left eye and clumsiness dropping her school pencils. On 2nd September, after her smile became suddenly lopsided during breakfast, she was rushed to Leeds General Infirmary.

The MRI revealed a 3.1 cm diffuse lesion filling her pons — the part of the brainstem that controls breathing, heartbeat and movement — with no safe surgical corridor. A stereotactic biopsy and molecular analysis confirmed the diagnosis: diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma, H3 K27M-mutant, WHO grade IV. Because of where it sits, surgeons cannot remove it.

sections.title: Standard Treatment and Its Limits
sections.content: Willow began a six-week course of focal radiotherapy (54 Gy in 30 fractions) at Leeds in late September, alongside steroids to control the swelling. Her doctors were honest with us: radiotherapy typically shrinks a DIPG for a few months, and median survival is 9–11 months. Fewer than 1 in 10 children survive two years. There is no standard chemotherapy that changes this — which is why every paediatric oncologist we spoke to said the same thing: get her onto a trial.

sections.title: The Hope: Trial Immunotherapy in Germany
sections.content:
After weeks of research and second opinions, Willow was accepted onto an individualised multimodal immunotherapy programme at a certified oncology centre in Germany, combining a personalised dendritic cell vaccine made from her own immune cells with targeted therapy matched to her tumour's H3 K27M mutation.

Early published reports describe objective responses in a subset of children with H3 K27M-mutant diffuse midline glioma treated with the targeted drug ONC201 (dordaviprone), and the German centre has confirmed it can begin Willow's programme in December — if we secure the funding. This programme is NOT funded by the NHS and is available only on a private-pay basis.

sections.title: Why We Need Your Help
sections.content: We want to be completely transparent. Willow's diagnosis, biopsy, radiotherapy and steroids were provided free of charge by the NHS at Leeds General Infirmary. That is covered. What is NOT available on the NHS is the trial immunotherapy programme in Germany — the only active treatment option her doctors can point to. We need £120,000 to get our six-year-old onto it before her window closes.

quote.text: She's six. She still loses teeth and believes the tooth fairy is late because of the hospital post. Her doctors told us the tumour can't be cut out — but there's a trial in Germany that could give her more birthdays. Every donation isn't just money — it's time. Time with her little brother. Time to be seven. Please help us get her there before December.
quote.author: Hannah R., Willow's mum

updates.title: Accepted onto the German programme 📋
updates.content: The biggest news so far: the centre in Germany has reviewed Willow's biopsy and MRI and confirmed her place on the trial immunotherapy programme, starting in December if we secure the funding. She is halfway through radiotherapy at Leeds and coping bravely. This is our window — please keep sharing.

updates.title: We've passed 1,100 donors! 🙏
updates.content: Your support has been overwhelming — more than 1,100 people have given. Willow finished her third week of radiotherapy and still insists on walking to school when she can. Her little brother drew a picture of 'the German doctors' for her hospital wall. Every pound brings us closer to December.

updates.title: Radiotherapy is underway
updates.content: Willow started her six-week course of radiotherapy at Leeds General Infirmary. She is dealing with tiredness and wobbliness, but her smile is intact. Her oncologist explained that radiotherapy buys time — which is exactly why the trial programme matters so much.

updates.title: The campaign has launched
updates.content: With heavy hearts but determination, we're launching this appeal. After the biopsy confirmed DIPG, her doctors told us clearly: standard treatment buys months, but the trial in Germany is her only active option. Unfortunately, it isn't funded by the NHS. We believe in the power of community.
